newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares seen rallying in run-up to budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares seen rallying in run-up to budget.

text.p: Speculative and investment bidding ahead of India's annual budget due at the end of the month will drive up share prices this week, brokers and analysts say.
"We expect the market to be in a firm bull grip by Wednesday," said Sanjay D'Souza, senior manager at Nucleus Securities. "We expect the market to rally to 3,550-3,575."
Last week the Bombay Stock Exchange's top-30 share index ended 24.75 points, or 0.73 percent, higher at 3,407.22 in unexciting trade.
"The past two-weeks have been a consolidating phase," said Ulhas Paymaster, a member-broker at the BSE. "People are going to now focus on the budget."
Indian finance minister P. Chidambaram is scheduled to unveil on February 28 the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March).
Analysts expect a flurry of activity in the 15 trading sessions before the budget, with foreign institutional investors and local funds and speculators taking positions.

"Media attention during this period will focus on potential market reforms and the budget package," D'Souza said. "This will build up expectations in market circles and bull operators and foreign institutional investors will drive up prices."
Vijay Pandya, a director at Classic Share and Stock Brokers, said market expectations were high for cuts in corporate taxes and incentives to boost retail investors.
"We see scope for a rise of 50-200 points (in the BSE index)," he said. "Fresh money is coming into the market."
"We predict a pre-budget level of 3,750 points," D'Souza said. "Any downside in the market should be construed as a mere short-term technical correction."
But Paymaster said budget expectations were tempered by caution because people knew that the government faced a tough task in tackling the budget deficit.
"There are conflicting interests at play -- the government needs to raise revenue; industry and the people want concessions," he said.
A likely increase in government-fixed prices of petroleum products was the major cause for concern, Paymaster added.
"It is inevitable. They will have to do it (raise product prices)," Sanjeev Patni, oil analyst at brokerage W.I Carr, told Reuters.

Government subsidy costs -- the difference between domestic prices of petroleum products and world prices -- will reach 155 billion rupees ($43 billion) by the end of fiscal 1996/97, petroleum ministry officials say.
Paymaster expects the government to raise oil prices which will in turn push up energy and transport costs for a wide range of industries.
"That's why I don't see a runaway market," he said. "One should ... book profits before the budget."
